newsitem.title: USA: Retiring boomers to boost Florida growth - report.
newsitem.headline: Retiring boomers to boost Florida growth - report.

text.p: Driven by a tremendous influx of older Americans, Florida will have strong gains in population, employmemt and income in the next 20 years, according to a report by DRI/McGraw-Hill.

"With its warm weather, pro-business climate and relatively low cost of living, Florida will compete head to head with Texas in the coming years for a share of the large number of ageing baby boomers entering into retirement," said the forecast, released Wednesday.

Florida is the fourth most-populous state in the nation. DRI/McGraw-Hill predicted it will replace New York as No. 3, behind California and Texas, over the next two decades as the U.S. population shifts from the Northeast and Midwest to the South and West.

Bolstered by population gains, Florida will be among the leaders nationally in job growth, with resident-driven services and trade employment remaining the greatest source of new jobs, the report said.

Florida's service sector, which accounts for more than 35 percent of its employment base, is expected to grow by 4.4 percent in 1997. Business services, including computer services and temporary employment, will post an especially strong gain of 7.5 percent this year, the forecast said.
Florida's tourism industry welcomed a record 42 million visitors to the state last year, partly because of spill-over from the Atlanta Olympics, new attractions and expanded airline flights.
"Amusement, recreation and lodging services will continue to thrive as rising incomes boost domestic and international tourism," said Sara Johnson, chief regional economist for DRI/McGraw-Hill.

The state's health services industry will see continued moderate job growth of 3 percent this year and 2.9 percent in 1998, and will rank as one of the strongest employment sectors through the rest of the 1990s, the report said.

Manufacturing growth will increase only modestly as companies continue to trim down in response to changing market conditions and increased competition from abroad. However, Florida will continue to benefit from increasing trade with Latin America as a rising volume of goods passes through the Gulf of Mexico.

The forecast said U.S. budget contraints will continue to hurt Florida's space industry and its defence contractors. But as many contractors move away from defence work and into consumer and commercial applications, the industry's payroll in the state will rise by 3.2 percent in 1997, above the national industry average of 2.3 percent.
